clinicalPearls: PID is infection and inflammation of the upper female genital tract, encompassing endometritis, salpingitis, oophoritis, tubo-ovarian abscess, and pelvic peritonitis
It is usually an ascending infection, most commonly caused by Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae, often with anaerobes and other vaginal flora
The clinical picture is variable and often subtle; classic findings are lower abdominal pain, deep dyspareunia, abnormal discharge, and cervical motion, uterine, or adnexal tenderness
Because sequelae are serious and diagnosis is imprecise, a low threshold for empirical treatment in at-risk women is recommended
Antibiotic regimens are broad-spectrum to cover gonococcus, chlamydia, and anaerobes; sexual partners should be evaluated and treated to prevent reinfection
Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome (perihepatitis) causes right upper quadrant pain and can mimic hepatobiliary disease
Intrauterine device users, recent instrumentation, and multiple sexual partners increase risk
Long-term consequences include tubal-factor infertility, ectopic pregnancy, and chronic pelvic pain, and risk rises with each recurrent episode
reference.pathophysiology: PID arises when micro-organisms ascend from the vagina and cervix through the endometrial cavity to the fallopian tubes and adjacent structures. Sexually transmitted pathogens, chiefly Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae, disrupt the cervical barrier and facilitate co-infection with endogenous aerobic and anaerobic vaginal flora. The resulting inflammation damages the tubal epithelium and cilia, leading to scarring, adhesions, and tubal occlusion. Progression can produce pyosalpinx, tubo-ovarian abscess, and pelvic peritonitis; spread to the hepatic capsule causes perihepatitis.
additionalDifferentials: Ovarian cyst accident (rupture, haemorrhage, or torsion)
Functional or irritable bowel-related pelvic pain
additionalInvestigations: Pregnancy test to exclude ectopic pregnancy
Endocervical or vaginal nucleic acid amplification testing for chlamydia and gonorrhoea
Microscopy and culture of genital tract samples
Inflammatory markers and full blood count
Pelvic ultrasound to detect tubo-ovarian abscess or pelvic collection
Laparoscopy when the diagnosis is uncertain or the patient fails to respond
redFlags: Signs of a tubo-ovarian abscess such as a tender adnexal mass with high fever
Peritonitis or suspicion of a ruptured abscess causing sepsis
Inability to tolerate oral therapy, pregnancy, or failure of outpatient treatment requiring admission
Severe right upper quadrant pain raising concern for perihepatitis or an alternative surgical diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Prompt, adequate antibiotic treatment usually resolves acute infection, but even treated PID carries appreciable risk of long-term tubal damage. Each recurrent episode further increases the likelihood of infertility, ectopic pregnancy, and chronic pelvic pain, so prevention and partner treatment are central to a good outcome.
pitfalls: Withholding treatment while awaiting definitive confirmation, allowing tubal damage to progress
Missing an ectopic pregnancy by not performing a pregnancy test
Neglecting to test for and treat sexual partners, leading to reinfection
Failing to recognise or drain a tubo-ovarian abscess
Assuming an absence of fever or normal inflammatory markers excludes PID
management: Start empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics covering gonococcus, chlamydia and anaerobes, typically ceftriaxone with doxycycline and metronidazole, with a low threshold for treatment given imprecise diagnosis and serious sequelae
Admit for intravenous therapy and consider drainage for severe disease, tubo-ovarian abscess, pregnancy or failure of oral treatment
Provide analgesia and advise rest, reassessing response and considering removal of an intrauterine device if there is no improvement
Notify, evaluate and treat sexual partners and advise abstinence until treatment is completed to prevent reinfection
Screen for coexisting sexually transmitted infections including HIV and offer contraception and safer-sex counselling
Exclude ectopic pregnancy and, where the diagnosis is uncertain or the patient fails to respond, consider laparoscopy
Counsel on the long-term risks of tubal infertility, ectopic pregnancy and chronic pelvic pain and arrange follow-up
